Numbers · Nov 4, 2026

How big is your state, really?

Most of us learned the world's sizes from a flat classroom map, and that map stretches everything far from the equator. Make a few guesses, then lay your state on top of any country at true size.

By Shawn Nafziger

Which is bigger?

Three quick ones. Tap the place you think has more .

Orange outline: the state. Gray: the country. Shapes: each drawn at true size, on the same scale. Guesses: counted as right or wrong, with no cookies and nothing that identifies you.

Lay your state on top

Pick a state and any country or territory. Both outlines are drawn at true size, on the same scale, with no map behind them to distort them. Drag your state around with a thumb or mouse.

Try:

Orange outline: your state. Gray: the country or territory. Shapes: each drawn at true size and as close to its true shape as a flat screen allows (). Outlines include lakes; the numbers count land only.

Orange dots: your state's people. Gray dots: the country's people. Dots: one dot = 100,000 people, spread evenly, not where people actually live.

Orange outline: your state. Gray: the country or territory. Line: the shortest path between their centers. Globe: drag to spin it.

Why do these sizes surprise people? The flat map on most classroom walls, called , stretches places more the farther they are from the equator. It makes Greenland look about 16 times its real size, which is why it seems as big as Africa. On a globe, nothing is stretched.

Your state among the world

Every state, country and territory on one line, from smallest to largest. 31 of the 50 states have more land than half of the 193 . Even Rhode Island, the smallest state, has more land than 27 of them, and Alaska has more than 175.

Tap a dot to see which place it is.

Orange: your state (pick it above). Blue: the other 49 states. Solid gray: countries. Hollow gray: territories. Scale: each step is 10 times the one before (). Counts: against the 193 UN member countries only.

Table: every place on the line

Every state's twin

Each state laid over the country or territory closest to it in size. Tap one to put it in the big view above.

Orange outline: the state. Gray: its twin. Twin: the country or territory closest to it in land area (or in people), measured as a ratio. Shapes: both at true size; each pair has its own scale.

How to read these "Land area" leaves out lakes, rivers and coastal water. Every outline is drawn at true size. That's why some look different from the map you know. "Territory" means a place governed by another country, like Greenland (Denmark) or Puerto Rico (U.S.). Each is labeled. "Twin" means the country or territory closest in land area (or people) to that state. Countries with far-off parts are measured as their main body ("mainland France"). Those parts appear on their own, like French Guiana.

Notes and sources

  • State land area: U.S. Census Bureau (TIGERweb, current boundaries).
  • Country and territory land area: World Bank (from FAO), latest year, mostly 2024.
  • Where the World Bank has no figure, or its border doesn't match the outline we draw, we measure the outline. Each of these places says so.
  • State population: U.S. Census Bureau, Vintage 2025 estimates, July 1, 2025.
  • Country and territory population: United Nations, World Population Prospects 2024, estimates for July 1, 2025 ().
  • Outlines: Census cartographic boundaries (states); Natural Earth (countries and territories), which follows the lines each government actually controls.
  • The list: the 193 UN member countries, plus Taiwan and Kosovo (not UN members) and Palestine (a UN observer state), and 39 territories that have their own UN population figure.
  • Rank counts ("more land than X countries") use the 193 UN members only, a list anyone can check.
  • Distances: the shortest path over the Earth's surface, between the centers of the two shapes.

Data: U.S. Census Bureau; World Bank (from FAO); UN DESA Population Division (World Population Prospects 2024). Outlines: U.S. Census Bureau; Natural Earth.
